target_customer: Consumers who want to play guitar songs without learning chords, buying a $299 guitar and paying for songs or a subscription
problem: Most people give up learning guitar because fretting chords is hard. The MI Guitar replaced the fretboard with buttons and a companion app so a beginner can play songs at once.
business_model: Hardware sale ($299 guitar) plus app content at $0.99 per song or about $6 per month
product_category: Consumer music hardware and learning app

founders.name: Brian Fan
founders.background_notes: YC page says he later became a senior product manager at Amazon Devices and Ring.

founders.name: Andrew Song
founders.background_notes: YC page mentions a cloud-based business background.

competitors.name: Jamstik
competitors.what: Connected guitar controller meant to help people become better guitarists

technical_complexity.rationale: A new consumer hardware product with a button fretboard, Bluetooth link, string sensing and a song app needed industrial design and manufacturing for a two or three person team, and shipping was planned for early 2017.

defensibility.rationale: The song library and app were proprietary but hardware concepts like the Yamaha EZ-AG and Fretlight already existed, and the company had no patents or network effects shown in sources.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent is documented as copying or buying it. The company's site now redirects to The Sound Junky, and CB Insights reports an August 2020 acquisition by that company, undisclosed terms.

market_need_then: Pre-orders were strong: the Indiegogo campaign reported about $415,000 and over 1,200 guitars pre-sold by mid 2016 (Designboom and others). Founder Fan described personal difficulty learning guitar.

branding.domain_note: magicinstruments.com, now redirecting to thesoundjunky.com (observed on fetch).

identity.visual_style: Designed with Ammunition (Designboom 2016-04-20); minimalist plastic guitar body
identity.voice_and_tone: Promise based and playful: 'Can't play a guitar? We guarantee you can play this one.'

branding.brand_signature: The guarantee line 'Can't play a guitar? We guarantee you can play this one.'
branding.community_and_virality: Widespread launch press in Engadget, Wired, TechCrunch, Design Milk and Gigazine in April 2016, plus an Indiegogo campaign and a Wefunder offer with 338 investors.

brand_strength.rationale: Strong launch press and crowdfunding response show the product and name travelled, but no evidence of lasting community or merch, and the company later disappeared into an acquirer.

outcome_analysis: Magic Instruments raised about $2M seed and over $400K in Indiegogo pre-orders in 2016, then a small Wefunder round in December 2016. Shipping was planned for early 2017, and nothing public shows later funding or sales scale. The YC page marks it inactive and CB Insights reports a quiet acquisition by The Sound Junky in 2020. No post-mortem exists, so the failure factor is an inference from the funding gap.
notes: The $2M seed rests on a Seedtable or StartupIntros entry and the company's own Wefunder page saying just under $2 million; investor names come from the database listing only. Indiegogo amounts vary by outlet ($397,300 to $415,000). CB Insights reports a total of $2,145,348. The acquisition by The Sound Junky (August 2020) rests on a single database and is consistent with the company domain redirecting to thesoundjunky.com. Other rivals named in company FAQ and launch posts as reported by search snippets only (Yamaha EZ-AG, Fretlight, gTar) were not opened and are not listed. crowdfundinsider page returned HTTP 403 on fetch.
